name: Rice root aphid on cannabis
summary: A primarily root-associated aphid of indoor Cannabis in North America. Direct, plant-linked root-colony evidence supports the pest class, while generalized decline, lower-leaf off-coloration, flying aphids, and sticky-card captures remain low-specificity cues. Species confirmation requires suitable intact specimens and expert morphology; root disease and irrigation stress must be evaluated independently.
affectedParts: stems and foliage during brief alate dispersal
upper-leaf trichomes that may trap dead alates
whole canopy for nonspecific secondary response
stages: post-harvest root system with living roots
indoor soil, aeroponic, coconut-coir, and rockwool production
indicators: Aphid colonies are visible on cannabis roots after careful root-zone inspection
Winged aphids emerge from or cluster around the growing medium while root colonies are present
Root-associated aphids are documented while stems and leaf undersides lack the typical cannabis-aphid colony pattern

Small temporary colonies may occur on stems or foliage after alates colonize a plant, but most observed offspring move downward toward roots and large persistent foliar colonies are atypical in the primary Cannabis account.
Dead alate aphids caught on upper-leaf hairs or low sticky cards can trigger root-zone inspection but cannot by themselves identify the infested plant or prove an active root colony.

Heavy infestation may coincide with generalized decline, reduced growth rate, or lower-leaf off-coloration; these canopy signs are supporting context only and have no unique rice-root-aphid morphology.
Root-associated aphids occur while leaf undersides, petioles, and stems lack the sustained foliar-colony pattern expected for cannabis aphid.
Repeated observations show colony or alate abundance changing on the same tagged plant; unrelated before-and-after images are not a progression series.
exclusions: Representative intact roots from the symptomatic plant are repeatedly inspected without aphids, cast skins, or a plausible colony while another measured cause explains the decline.
Dense persistent aphid colonies occupy stems, petioles, or leaf undersides and suitable morphology supports cannabis aphid or another foliar aphid.
A yellow sticky card contains a dark winged insect but the root zone is not linked, the specimen is too small for aphid morphology, or fungus gnats and other flyers are mixed on the card.
Small dark flies plus translucent, dark-headed larvae in moist media support fungus gnats rather than root aphids.
Springtails, soil mites, shore flies, thrips, whiteflies, or other root-zone arthropods are identified from the observed organisms.
Brown, slimy, sloughed, or odorous roots occur without plant-linked aphids and oomycete testing or root-zone oxygen evidence supports Pythium or hypoxia.
Root galls, cysts, females, or egg masses plus nematode evidence support root-knot nematodes rather than aphid feeding.
Canopy decline follows a measured pH, EC, moisture, temperature, root-restriction, nutrient, vascular, or pathogen pattern and the insects are absent or incidental.

progression.description: Record incoming plant lot, root condition, production medium, nearby crop age, sticky-card counts, and matched apparently unaffected plants before a colony is detected.
Aphids remain largely hidden on roots or near the stem base; canopy appearance may still be normal and canopy-only scouting can miss the infestation.
More root-associated nymphs, adults, and cast skins become visible across the tagged root zone; quantify inspected root area and organism counts instead of inferring density from one macro image.
Winged females may emerge from soil, particularly as Cannabis flowers or approaches maturity, and may appear on stems, foliage, trichomes, or low sticky cards before offspring move toward roots.

General decline, slower growth, or lower-leaf off-coloration may accompany high numbers, but root decay, pathogen involvement, yield loss, and causality remain separate questions requiring matched measurements.

lookAlikes: Bird cherry-oat aphid or another Rhopalosiphum species
Thrips or whitefly alates on sticky cards
Pythium or another oomycete root rot
Root binding, pH stress, or salinity / high EC
confirmation: Capture a traceable sequence from the same plant: whole canopy, labeled container and medium surface, root crown, representative exposed roots, colony overview, and macro or microscope views with a scale.

Record plant ID, cultivar, stage, production system, source lot, onset date, irrigation and root-zone history, root condition, inspected root area, aphid counts, alate counts, and sticky-card position and date.
Preserve intact apterous adults and representative alates in a manner suitable for entomological identification; do not rely on color, a single nymph, or a low-resolution sticky-card silhouette.
Use a qualified entomologist and appropriate morphological keys or validated molecular identification when a species-level Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale label is required.
Inspect leaf undersides, petioles, and stems for sustained cannabis-aphid colonies, and compare fungus-gnat adults and larvae when flyers are the initial cue.

Assess root color, firmness, odor, oxygen/moisture status, pH, EC, root restriction, and representative pathogen or nematode samples independently; finding aphids does not prove they caused every root or canopy symptom.

Keep canopy-only, damage-only, sticky-card-only, alate-only, organism-only, unlinked-root, mixed-arthropod, low-resolution, stock, vendor, generated, anecdotal, forum, and unverified observations out of the confirmed class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Preserve plant-linked root and insect evidence before treatment or destructive root washing.
Inspect nearby plants and incoming propagation lots using the same root-zone protocol and isolate confirmed infestations where practical.
Record root disease and irrigation evidence separately so concurrent problems are not collapsed into one label.
correctivePlan: Use an integrated root-zone pest-management response based on confirmed identity, population, production system, crop stage, and locally legal options.
Verify response by repeated plant-linked root inspection and alate counts; fewer flyers alone do not demonstrate that root colonies are absent.
If root or canopy decline continues after aphid numbers fall, continue the independent root-zone, nutrition, and pathogen workup.
prevention: Inspect roots of incoming clones, rooted cuttings, and retained mother material before integration.
Separate new plantings from older flowering or near-maturity plants that may be producing dispersing alates.
Use dated low-position sticky cards as an early cue while retaining scheduled direct root inspection as the confirmation method.
Avoid reusing containers or media with living roots from an infested crop without a validated sanitation process.
warnings: Photo or video alone cannot confirm rice root aphid to species; even a clear root-colony image needs a plant link and suitable organism evidence.
Generalized decline, slow growth, lower-leaf discoloration, and flying aphids are not unique symptoms and must not be used as ground truth without a documented root colony.
The primary Cannabis article states that increased pathogen susceptibility remains unconfirmed; root discoloration or decay must be labeled and tested independently.
The cited 2020 article and UNH guide reported indoor high-THC Cannabis associations and no North American outdoor-hemp records; that evidence gap does not prove outdoor infestation is impossible.

The existing CC BY 4.0 reference is one aeroponic root-crown figure. It remains training-ineligible pending source-group review and does not represent soil, coir, rockwool, cultivar, stage, geography, or severity diversity.
No verified diagnostic video or matched Cannabis progression series is included.

sources.title: Cannabis sativa as a Host of Rice Root Aphid (Hemiptera: Aphididae) in North America
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press on behalf of the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Indoor Cannabis sativa has emerged as a common North American host of rice root aphid, Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale.

The authors observed rice root aphid in Cannabis soil, aeroponic, coconut-coir, and rockwool systems, but had not found it in outdoor hemp plantings; the outdoor evidence gap must not be converted into an absence claim.

In indoor Cannabis the aphid is almost entirely root-associated; alate females can emerge from soil especially during flowering and near maturity, colonize new plants, and produce young on stems or foliage before most offspring migrate downward.
Dead alates trapped on upper-leaf hairs can be an early facility-level cue, but a sticky-card or canopy alate is not plant-linked confirmation of a root colony.
Heavy Cannabis infestations were associated with generalized decline, slower growth, and possible lower-leaf off-coloration, none of which is unique to rice root aphid.
The article explicitly states that a Cannabis association with increased pathogen susceptibility still requires confirmation; root discoloration or decay must therefore be diagnosed independently.

sources.title: Hemp Pests in New Hampshire
sources.organization: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
sources.publisher: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
supportedClaims: UNH Extension associates Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale with indoor Cannabis sativa grown as a high-THC crop and reports observations from indoor cultivation across the United States.

The institutional guide reported no North American outdoor-hemp records and identified hemp soil-insect research as a gap; this supports an indoor-production scope flag rather than proof that outdoor infestation is impossible.
